placeholders.inCon: Get-there: ', still in <constellation>' or ', in <constellation>' for the stop being reached (empty for the first stop).
placeholders.ifUp: Guard, renders as nothing: the variant is used only when {next}'s value is clearly larger than {prev}'s (ranges do not overlap).
placeholders.ifDown: Guard, renders as nothing: only when {next}'s value is clearly smaller than {prev}'s (ranges do not overlap).
placeholders.ifClear: Guard, renders as nothing: only when the two values clearly differ (ranges do not overlap, ratio at least 1.5).
placeholders.ifSimilar: Guard, renders as nothing: only when the two values' published ranges overlap.
placeholders.prev: Display name of the previous stop (in skip lines: the last stop actually seen).
placeholders.next: Display name of the stop being arrived at.
placeholders.name: Display name of the stop the line is about (compare.*, why.*, payoff.*). In story.* lines: the payoff stop, empty after an archetype switch (so only name-free story variants fit).
placeholders.hook: Display name of the journey's first stop (callbacks, payoffs and story lines).
placeholders.skipped: Display name of the stop the observer skipped or could not find.
placeholders.prevVal: Formatted value of the link's property for {prev}, number plus unit with no 'about' (e.g. '3,600 K', '650 million years'). The property is the edge subtype when it is a FactKey, otherwise the first factRef's fact. Rendered from a sourced FactValue; a range renders as '550–650 light-years'.
placeholders.value: Formatted value of the card number being compared (compare.* lines), number plus unit.
placeholders.ratioPhrase: Rounded ratio with a comparative, e.g. 'about 3 times hotter', 'about 20 times farther'. In transitions it compares {next} with {prev}; in compare.* lines it compares the value with the Sun.
placeholders.scaled: Value rendered on the app-wide scale model where the Sun is a 1 cm marble: size → the object's diameter (e.g. '7.6 m'); distance → km at 68 km per light-year (e.g. '92,000 km'); time.sun-day → age ÷ 4,600 million years × 24 h (e.g. '30 minutes').
placeholders.year: Calendar year the light now arriving left the object of the line ({next} in transitions, {name} elsewhere): current year minus distanceLy, rounded to the decade above 100 ly and to the century above 1,000 ly; written '1470', '680 CE' or '5500 BCE'.
placeholders.ago: Light-travel time of the same object as a duration: 'about 25,000 years', '2.5 million years'.
placeholders.deg: Angular distance of the hop in degrees, rounded.
placeholders.fields: Hop distance in fields of the selected binoculars (distance ÷ true field), as words: 'half a', 'one', 'one and a half'.
placeholders.screenDir: Direction to move in the observer's view: 'up', 'down and to the left', and so on.
placeholders.compassHint: Optional tail starting with ', ' naming the constellation the hop enters (e.g. ', toward Taurus'), or empty.
placeholders.anchor: Display name of the naked-eye anchor star for a naked-eye hop.
placeholders.region: Patch label, e.g. 'Orion' or 'the Summer Triangle'.
placeholders.theme: Title of the template the journey switches into (switch.* lines).
placeholders.bridge: The Concept.bridge sentence of the concept the observer missed (skip.bridge, bridge.prereq).
placeholders.claim: Superlative claim without its scope, e.g. 'one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye' (why.superlative; noun-phrase claims) or a full statement (why.superlative.statement). The scope stays in the card details.
placeholders.question: The journey's driving question as rendered. Available to why.hook lines, but the shipped bank never repeats it: the UI shows it on the overview and, for the first stop without its own card.question, in the question box.
placeholders.kind: Plain kind of the stop the line is about, with its article: 'an orange giant', 'a young open cluster' (plain-language.ts plainKind).
placeholders.prevKind: Plain kind of {prev} with its article ('an orange giant'). Filled only when it differs from {next}'s kind.
placeholders.nextKind: Plain kind of {next} with its article. Filled only when it differs from {prev}'s kind.
placeholders.sharedKind: The plain kind {prev} and {next} share, with its article ('an open cluster'). Filled only when the two kinds are the same.
placeholders.themeQuestion: Driving question of the template the journey switches into (switch.* lines).
placeholders.span: Hop length in binocular fields of the selected instrument plus degrees: 'about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (13°)'.
placeholders.fov: True field of the selected binoculars in degrees, e.g. '6.5'.
placeholders.anchorLook: Anchor star with a recognizable description: 'Arcturus, the bright orange star of Boötes,' (ends with a comma when described), or 'Alphecca in Corona Borealis'.

hook.A1-cradle-to-grave: One patch of sky holds every chapter of a star's life, from cold cloud to cinders.
Stars are born, grow old and die, and tonight you can see all three in a few sweeps.
The gas a dying star gives back becomes the next stars, and you can follow the cycle.
hook.A2-thermometer: A star's color is its temperature, and your eyes can read it like a thermometer.
In the sky red means cool and blue means hot, the reverse of every bathroom tap.
A gentle defocus turns tonight's stars into embers and sparks, each a temperature.
hook.A3-how-far: The brightest stars are not always the nearest, and tonight you find out which are.
Start with a star next door and climb outward, each rung farther than the last.
No one has traveled to a star, yet we know how far they are; tonight you see how.
hook.A4-time-machine: Every point of light is a letter posted long ago, each one sent at a different time.
Looking farther means looking back in time, and each stop tonight shows older light.
The light in your binoculars left these stars in different centuries of our history.
hook.A5-families: Stars are born in litters from one cloud, then slowly wander away from their siblings.
The Sun lost track of its siblings long ago, but many stars still travel with theirs.
From tight young clusters to scattered families, tonight shows how star families age.
hook.A6-contrasts: Stars that pass for twins can be strangers, and one hidden fact gives them away.
Neighbors on the sky can be worlds apart in age, size or distance.
Two stars can look alike and live opposite lives; tonight you find what parts them.
hook.A7-record-breakers: The sky's record holders are within binocular reach, and every record has a cause.
Some of the most extreme objects in the galaxy hide among ordinary-looking stars.
Each stop tonight is a record holder, extreme for a physical reason you can name.
hook.A8-how-stars-die: A star dies gently or violently, and its weight makes the choice.
Some stars fade inside a smoke ring and others explode; one fate awaits the Sun.
Tonight you see what is left when stars die, and learn which ending the Sun will get.
hook.A9-seeing-double: Many single-looking stars split in two in binoculars, and some pairs are real partners.
A single point of light can hold a whole family of stars circling one another.
Some pairs are bound by gravity and others are strangers lined up by chance.
hook.A10-stars-that-change: Some stars swell, fade and wink, and you can judge their brightness yourself.
Stars look steady, yet some are pulsing, eclipsing or hiding behind their own dust.
Spend a night as a variable-star observer, comparing stars that refuse to keep still.
hook.A11-inside-our-galaxy: We live inside a galaxy, and tonight you look along its disk, above it and beyond it.
The Milky Way's glow is our own galaxy seen edge-on from within.
From the crowded disk to the halo and beyond, tonight traces our galactic address.
hook.A12-moonlit: Moonlight drowns faint nebulae, but it cannot touch color, doubles or bright clusters.
A bright Moon is no enemy of star colors and double stars, which it cannot wash out.
The Moon steals the faint things tonight, so the night belongs to color and pairs.
payoff.A1-cradle-to-grave: Stars condense out of cold clouds, shine on the fuel in their cores, and finally hand their gas back to space, where it builds new stars and planets, ours among them.
From {hook} to {name}, nothing in a star's life is wasted: what a dying star gives back becomes new stars and planets, and some of it, long ago, became us.
A star is born from a collapsing cloud, lives on its fuel and dies by returning its gas to space. The Sun and Earth are built from the leftovers of that cycle.
payoff.A2-thermometer: Color is temperature: {hook} glows at the cool, ember end and {name} at the hot, blue-white end, and your eyes alone can read the whole scale.
Stars differ in color because their surfaces differ in temperature, cool ones orange-red like {hook} and the hottest blue-white like {name}, just as a heated poker goes from red to white.
You have just read a thermometer stretched across the sky, from the ember glow of {hook} to the blue-white blaze of {name}, using only the color of their light.
payoff.A3-how-far: {hook} was the nearest and {name} the farthest, its light taking about {ago} to reach you. Brightness alone would never have told you that order, but measurement did.
Astronomers measure the nearest stars by parallax, a star's small shift as Earth circles the Sun, and reach as far as {name} with cleverer yardsticks built on that first step.
The order runs from {hook}, nearest, out to {name}, farthest, and every rung of that ladder was measured rather than guessed, each method resting on the one before it.
payoff.A4-time-machine: The light from {name} set out about {ago} ago, the oldest of the night, and it reached your eye in the same moment as the far younger light of {hook}.
The freshest light tonight came from {hook} and the oldest from {name}, which left it around {year}: letters posted at different times, all arriving together.
Every stop showed a different moment of the past, and {name} reaches back furthest: its light has crossed empty space for about {ago} to meet you.
payoff.A5-families: Stars are born in families from one cloud and drift apart as they age, as the Sun's own siblings did long ago; they are still out there, circling the galaxy.
From the close-knit family of {hook} to the looser one of {name}, the pattern is clear: star families start tight and spread out with time.
Every star was born into a family, and most families slowly scatter; {name} shows one well along that road, and the Sun's own family went the same way long ago.
payoff.A6-contrasts: One hidden property, whether temperature, age, distance or mass, set each pair apart even when they looked alike, and {name} showed how wide that gap can be.
Each pair tonight shared a look and differed in one deep way, which is why astronomers measure stars instead of trusting their appearance.
What your eye sees, color and brightness, is only the surface; underneath, each look-alike pair differed in temperature, age, distance or mass, and that difference shaped their lives.
payoff.A7-record-breakers: The most extreme sight of the night was {name}, and none of the records was an accident: each came from mass, age or sheer distance.
From {hook} to {name}, every record holder is extreme for a physical reason, and the remarkable thing is that ordinary binoculars reach them all.
Extremes are where physics shows its hand: {name} tops tonight's list, and its record, like all the others, has a cause you can name.
payoff.A8-how-stars-die: The Sun is too light to explode: it will swell into a giant, puff off a glowing shell and settle as a white dwarf, while only far heavier stars end like {name}.
The Sun's ending will be gentle, a giant, then a glowing shell, then a slowly cooling white dwarf, and {name} shows the violent fate kept for much heavier stars.
Mass decides how a star dies: Sun-like stars fade inside glowing shells, while the heavyweights end in a supernova, as {name} shows, scattering the makings of new worlds.
payoff.A9-seeing-double: {name} looks like a single star to the eye, yet it holds a whole system, several stars sharing one point of light.
Some pairs are true partners and some only line up by chance, and {name} is the real thing, stars held together by gravity and circling one another.
Your eye counted one star, binoculars and physics counted more, and {name} is the proof that a single point of light can be a crowd.
payoff.A10-stars-that-change: None of tonight's stars keeps still, and each changes for its own reason: swelling and shrinking, a partner passing in front, or dust drifting across its face.
Stars do change, and usefully: the strict rhythm of a Cepheid, a star that swells and shrinks like a slow heartbeat, even tells astronomers how far away it is.
Every change you saw was a clue, a pulse, an eclipsing partner or a veil of dust, and patient watchers have turned such clues into physics.
payoff.A11-inside-our-galaxy: We live inside the flat disk you swept at the start, wrapped in an ancient halo, and {name} took you farther from home than anything else tonight.
Our address is the Milky Way's disk: you looked along it, then out of it, and finally across the gulf to {name}.
We live in the disk among nurseries and star clusters, and {name} shows how far the view reaches beyond them.
payoff.A12-moonlit: Even under a bright Moon, color, double stars and bright clusters come through untouched, and {name} proves it.
Moonlight washed out the faint nebulae and galaxies tonight, but not {name}, nor the colors and pairs that came before it.
Plenty survives moonlight, star colors, double stars and bright families of stars among it, with {name} as tonight's proof.
switch.A1-cradle-to-grave: How a star's story ends depends on its weight. {themeQuestion}
Now that you have seen a star near its end, the ending itself deserves a closer look. {themeQuestion}
switch.A2-thermometer: Color also hints at age, since the reddest giants are old stars near their end. {themeQuestion}
A star's color is a clue to its whole life, not just its temperature. {themeQuestion}
switch.A3-how-far: Distance is also time, because the farther the stop, the older the light you are seeing. {themeQuestion}
Every light-year is also a year that the light spent on the road. {themeQuestion}
switch.A4-time-machine: All those ages rest on distances, and distances have to be measured somehow. {themeQuestion}
To date old light you first need to know how far it came. {themeQuestion}
switch.A5-families: Families grow old, and so do the stars in them. {themeQuestion}
A family's age shows in its stars, and that leads to their whole life story. {themeQuestion}
switch.A6-contrasts: Of all the contrasts, color is the one your eye reads best, and it turns out to be a thermometer. {themeQuestion}
The sharpest contrast in the sky is color, and color has a cause. {themeQuestion}
switch.A7-record-breakers: Extremes invite comparison, and some of the strongest contrasts sit side by side. {themeQuestion}
Records only mean something next to ordinary stars. {themeQuestion}
switch.A8-how-stars-die: Dead stars seed new ones, so the story circles back to its beginning. {themeQuestion}
Every stellar ending feeds a new beginning. {themeQuestion}
switch.A9-seeing-double: Some pairs do more than sit together: they eclipse each other, and their light changes. {themeQuestion}
A double star that eclipses becomes a variable star. {themeQuestion}
switch.A10-stars-that-change: A steady pulse can serve as a ruler for distance. {themeQuestion}
Pulsing stars turned out to be measuring rods for the universe. {themeQuestion}
switch.A11-inside-our-galaxy: Looking out of our galaxy also means looking back in time. {themeQuestion}
Light from that far away is old light. {themeQuestion}
switch.A12-moonlit: The colors you have been seeing are a thermometer in disguise. {themeQuestion}
Moonlight leaves color alone, and color is temperature. {themeQuestion}

story.A1-cradle-to-grave: A star's life runs from a cold cloud to a glowing wreck. Tonight you follow it forward through the sky around {region}, from {hook} to {name}.
Stars are not eternal: they condense out of cold clouds, shine on the fuel in their cores, and give their gas back when they die. Tonight each chapter is a different object.
Nothing in a star's life is wasted. The gas a dying star returns to space becomes the next generation, and tonight's stops follow that cycle from start to finish.
story.A2-thermometer: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white. Stars follow the same rule, and tonight you line them up from the warm glow of {hook} to the blue-white of {name}.
A star's color is a direct reading of its surface temperature, no instrument needed. Tonight's stops climb from cool toward hot, so compare each color with the last.
Red stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars the scorching ones, which surprises almost everyone. A gentle defocus makes the colors easier to judge, starting with {hook}.
story.A3-how-far: Brightness is a poor guide to distance, since a modest star nearby can outshine a giant far away. Tonight you climb outward from {hook}, each stop farther than the last.
Each rung of tonight's ladder lies farther than the last. Near stars give away their distance by a tiny shift as Earth circles the Sun; the far ones need cleverer tricks built on that.
You start close to home with {hook} and step outward through {region}. By the end, the depth of the sky is something you can feel.
story.A4-time-machine: Light is fast but not instant, so everything you see in the sky is already history. Each stop tonight shows older light than the last, from {hook} out to {name}.
The light entering your binoculars set out long before you looked up, and from each stop at a different time. Read the night like a calendar, starting with {hook}, the freshest light.
Every distance in the sky is also a stretch of time. Starting with {hook}, you move to ever older light, and the night becomes a walk back through history.
story.A5-families: Stars are born in batches from a single cloud, then slowly drift apart. Tonight you meet families of different ages, from {hook} to {name}, and watch the ties loosen.
Somewhere in the galaxy the Sun's brothers and sisters are still out there, scattered beyond recognition. Tonight's star families show how that happens, starting with {hook}.
A star cluster is a family photograph: siblings born together from one cloud, all sharing a birthday. Look at a few and a story appears, of families that start tight and slowly come apart.
story.A6-contrasts: Two stars can share a patch of sky, a color or a brightness and still be strangers. Tonight's game is finding the hidden fact that sets each pair apart.
Looks deceive in the sky as much as anywhere. Starting at {hook}, you compare neighbors that seem alike and find the one difference that gave them such different lives.
The sky looks flat, so stars that seem like neighbors or twins can be anything but. Tonight is a game of spot-the-difference, played with real physics.
story.A7-record-breakers: Among the ordinary-looking stars hide some of the most extreme objects your eyes will ever catch. Tonight you visit them from {hook} to {name}, and every record has a reason.

Every record in the sky, whether the biggest star, the brightest or the farthest light, comes from something physical: mass, age or sheer distance. Tonight you collect the records and their reasons together.
Extremes are where physics shows its hand most clearly. Starting with {hook}, each stop holds a record, and each record has a cause you can name.
story.A8-how-stars-die: Stars die in one of two ways, and which one depends above all on how heavy the star was at birth. By {name} you will know which ending awaits the Sun.
A Sun-like star ends quietly, puffing its outer layers into space, while a heavyweight tears itself apart in a supernova. Tonight you see what both endings leave behind, starting with {hook}.
The Sun will not last forever, and the sky is full of stars that have already reached the end. Tonight's stops show the two ways a star can go, and why weight decides.
story.A9-seeing-double: Many stars that look single to the eye split into pairs in binoculars, and some pairs hold whole families. Count them from {hook} onward, and ask which pairs really belong together.
A double star can be a true couple, two suns circling each other, or two strangers that happen to line up. Tonight's stops include both kinds, and telling them apart is half the pleasure.
Your eye sees one point of light, binoculars sometimes see two, and physics often finds more. From {hook} to {name}, tonight is an exercise in counting stars that hide behind one another.
story.A10-stars-that-change: The stars look as steady as streetlights, yet some swell and shrink, some are eclipsed by a partner, and some fade behind their own dust. Tonight you watch them as a variable-star observer would.
Starting with {hook}, you visit stars whose brightness will not sit still. Each changes for its own physical reason, and you can judge the change yourself against the stars nearby.
Flickering stars have taught astronomers a remarkable amount, including how far away other galaxies are. Tonight you meet a few of them and learn to estimate their brightness by eye.
story.A11-inside-our-galaxy: We see the Milky Way from inside, a little like a fish trying to picture its pond. Tonight you look along the crowded disk, up toward the halo, and out of the galaxy to {name}.
The faint band of the Milky Way is our galaxy seen edge-on from within. From {hook} onward, tonight's stops trace where we live: in the disk, inside an ancient halo, with other galaxies beyond.
Every star you can see without a telescope belongs to our own galaxy, most of them to its thin disk. Tonight you work outward from that disk to see how far the view reaches.
story.A12-moonlit: A bright Moon washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, but not a star's color, a double's split or a bright cluster's sparkle. Tonight is built from exactly those.
Moonlit nights have their own treasures. Starting with {hook}, tonight's stops were chosen to shine through the glare, and each holds up well in it.
Moonlight steals the faint and delicate things, but leaves color, pairs and bright star families alone. Tonight is a tour of what the Moon cannot spoil, ending at {name}.
